title: Some Non-Hashable Objects still Work as Auxiliary Data in Custom Pytree
question:
I make a custom pytree like this. I want to know how auxiliary data works in pytree.
Copy
@jax.tree_util.register_pytree_node_class
class A:

    def __init__(self):
        self.a = jax.numpy.ones((3,))
        self.b = jax.numpy.ones((3,))

    def tree_flatten(self):
        return (self.a,), (self.b,)

    @classmethod
    def tree_unflatten(cls, aux_data, children):
        obj = cls.__new__(cls)
        obj.a = children[0]
        obj.b = aux_data[0]
        return obj

x1 = A()
x2 = A()

t1 = jax.tree_util.tree_structure(x1)
t2 = jax.tree_util.tree_structure(x2)

t1 == t2
The code above raises the error below, as expected:
Copy
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/yahya/Projects/coba/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/jax/_src/array.py", line 295, in __bool__
    core.check_bool_conversion(self)
  File "/home/yahya/Projects/coba/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/jax/_src/core.py", line 941, in check_bool_conversion
    raise ValueError("The truth value of an array with more than one element"
ValueError: The truth value of an array with more than one element is ambiguous. Use a.any() or a.all()

The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/yahya/Projects/coba/main.py", line 46, in <module>
    t1 == t2
ValueError: Exception raised while checking equality of metadata fields of pytree node of type <class '__main__.A'>. Make sure that metadata fields are hashable and have simple equality semantics. (Note: arrays cannot be passed as metadata fields!)
I expect that because the doc says "Auxiliary data becomes part of the treedef, which JAX compares and hashes (for example, when deciding whether two pytrees have the same structure), so it must support meaningful equality and hashing." which is the array type is not hashable.
But, when I changed self.b = jax.numpy.ones((3,)) to self.b = [1] then no error is raised. I expect that it will raise an error because the list object is not hashable. I hope someone here can give me explanation about this.
answers:
This is discussed at https://github.com/jax-ml/jax/issues/28659#issuecomment-2902750811, as well as at https://github.com/jax-ml/jax/issues/24204.
The short answer to why you're seeing this behavior is that while it's true that aux_data must be hashable, for performance reasons JAX doesn't preemptively validate hashability, and also for performance reasons the hashability may not be exercised in any particular pytree operation.
Still, you should avoid non-hashable aux_data because it can cause subtle problems in general; for example:
Copy
@jax.jit
def get_b(x):
  return jnp.asarray(x.b)

x1 = A()
print(get_b(x1))
# [1]

x1.b.append(2)  # mutate static value
print(get_b(x1))  # jit uses cached computation
# [1]
Since the code has violated the assumption that aux_data is hashable (and thus immutable by Python's requirements for hashability), JIT ends up silently producing unexpected results.

title: How to visualize a Jax neural network?
question:
Just as there are several tools to visualise Pytorch models as discussed here, what tools can we use to visualise a neural network built with Jax? The goal would be to visualise the neural network as a directed acyclic graph of nodes passing tensors to each other as it happens during the forward pass. Furthermore, as Jax supports parallelism through sharding as a first-class concept, are there tools that visualise this as well?
For example,
import jax.numpy as jnp
from flax import nnx

class MLP(nnx.Module):
    def __init__(self, rngs):
        self.dense0 = nnx.Linear(8, 16, rngs=rngs)
        self.dense1 = nnx.Linear(16, 4, rngs=rngs)

    def __call__(self, x):
        x = self.dense0(x)
        x = nnx.relu(x)
        x = self.dense1(x)
        return x


model = MLP(nnx.Rngs(0))
example_input = jnp.ones((1, 8))

# Call tool to visualize it here
Should produce something like
input
 (1, 8)
    │
┌───▼───────────────────────────┐
│ MLP                           │
│ dense0 ──(1, 16)──▶ relu      │
│                    │          │
│                 (1, 16)       │
│                    ▼          │
│                 dense1        │
└────────────────────│──────────┘
                  (1, 4)
                     ▼
                   output
answers:
I ended up creating a tool for this called jaxviz to produce interactive visualizations within notebooks.
Here is a usage of it on a simple MLP with sharding:
import jax
from jaxviz import trace_model

jax.config.update("jax_num_cpu_devices", 8)

import jax.numpy as jnp
from flax import nnx


Auto = jax.sharding.AxisType.Auto
mesh = jax.make_mesh(
    (8,),
    ("model",),
    axis_types=(Auto,),
    devices=jax.devices("cpu"),
)


class MLP(nnx.Module):
    def __init__(self, rngs):
        init = nnx.initializers.lecun_normal()
        self.dense0 = nnx.Linear(
            32,
            64,
            use_bias=False,
            kernel_init=nnx.with_partitioning(init, (None, "model")),
            rngs=rngs,
        )
        self.dense1 = nnx.Linear(
            64,
            32,
            use_bias=False,
            kernel_init=nnx.with_partitioning(init, ("model", None)),
            rngs=rngs,
        )

    def __call__(self, x):
        x = self.dense0(x)
        x = nnx.relu(x)
        return self.dense1(x)


@jax.jit
def create_model():
    return MLP(nnx.Rngs(0))


with jax.set_mesh(mesh):
    model = create_model()
    example_input = jax.device_put(jnp.ones((16, 32)), jax.P(None, None))
    trace_model(model, example_input, view='global')
It can also show the per-device view (useful when the modell uses sharding) with the view flag
with jax.set_mesh(mesh):
    model = create_model()
    example_input = jax.device_put(jnp.ones((16, 32)), jax.P(None, None))
    trace_model(model, example_input, view='per_device')
Here are some examples I traced: https://sachinhosmani.github.io/jaxviz/
